issues.legal_issue: Land acquisition proceedings do not lapse for failure to make an award within the prescribed period after possession has been taken under the urgency procedure and the land has vested in the government.
material_facts: The acquisition was initiated using the urgency procedure, and possession of the acquired land was taken under Section 17(1).
The challengers contended that the proceedings had lapsed because an award had not been made within the period prescribed by Section 11-A.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition proceedings did not lapse because possession had been taken and the land had vested in the government; Section 11-A did not apply even if no award had been made within its prescribed period.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 11-A, 17(1) and 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, read together, establish that Section 11-A ordinarily protects landowners where the acquisition remains pending and title has not vested in the government. Once possession is taken under Section 17(1), the land vests absolutely in the government, and the Act provides no mechanism for it to revert to the owner. The Court applied the rule stated in State of U.P. v. S.P. Jain, 1993 (4) SCC 369.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and urgency_possession_taken and land_vested_in_government and award_not_made_in_time

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns proceedings to acquire land for a public purpose.
predicates.urgency_possession_taken: The government took possession of the land before an award under the ordinary procedure was made, relying on an urgency procedure.
predicates.land_vested_in_government: Taking possession caused the land to vest in the government.
predicates.award_not_made_in_time: No award was made within the applicable statutory period.

issues.definition: When an acquisition proceeding involves urgency possession that vests the land in the government, failure to make an award within the applicable period does not cause the proceedings to lapse.

issues.legal_issue: A land-acquisition proceeding that substantially contains the elements of an award may be treated as an award even if it is not in the prescribed form.
material_facts: A prior court order directed the Collector to prepare an award in the acquisition proceedings.

The Collector issued a proceeding dated 31 July 1984 containing the requisites of an award and bearing the Collector's signature, although the signature was illegible and the proceeding was not in Form 15.
The challengers disputed that the proceeding was an award, while the society sought implementation of the earlier court order.
issues.conclusion: The proceeding was in substance an award, although it was not in Form 15, and the authority could be directed to sign and complete it in accordance with the earlier order.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 requires the Collector to make an award under the Collector's hand and sets out the award's substantive contents. The Court treated compliance with the prescribed form as procedural where the proceeding contained the requisites of an award. It also upheld the High Court's authority under Article 215 to issue directions in the circumstances, including where conduct potentially called for contempt proceedings.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and prior_court_order_requires_award and proceeding_contains_award_requisites and proceeding_not_in_prescribed_form

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns proceedings to acquire land.
predicates.prior_court_order_requires_award: A court had previously directed the responsible authority to prepare an award in the acquisition proceedings.
predicates.proceeding_contains_award_requisites: The authority issued a proceeding containing the substantive elements of an award.
predicates.proceeding_not_in_prescribed_form: The issued proceeding did not use the prescribed form.

issues.definition: A proceeding in an acquisition matter is treated as an award when it contains the award's substantive elements despite not using the prescribed form, where a prior court order required an award.

issues.legal_issue: The existence of other proceedings does not bar a writ seeking implementation of earlier court directions when the writ's principal relief is distinct from relief sought in those proceedings.
material_facts: The society had filed an encroachment application and a civil suit concerning removal of encroachments and restoration of possession.
The society's writ petition principally sought implementation of directions in an earlier judgment, with relief concerning encroachments being consequential or incidental.
The earlier judgment had upheld the acquisition and directed the Collector to prepare an award.
issues.conclusion: The other proceedings did not justify denying the writ relief, because the writ principally sought implementation of the earlier court directions rather than the same relief sought in the other proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 confers discretionary writ jurisdiction. Ordinarily, a litigant cannot pursue parallel remedies for the same matter, as reflected in Jai Singh v. Union of India, AIR 1977 SC 898. But the rule does not require a court to withhold relief in an exceptional situation where the writ seeks implementation of prior court orders and those orders are being thwarted; consequential or incidental relief does not make the principal relief the same as that sought in other proceedings.

predicates.writ_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding seeking relief under the court's writ jurisdiction.
predicates.alternative_proceedings_exist: The applicant has also initiated other legal proceedings concerning related facts.
predicates.writ_seeks_implementation_of_prior_court: The principal relief sought in the writ is to give effect to directions made in an earlier court judgment.
predicates.alternative_proceedings_seek_distinct_re: The other proceedings principally seek relief different from the implementation sought in the writ.

issues.definition: Other proceedings do not bar writ relief when the writ principally seeks implementation of earlier court directions and the other proceedings seek distinct relief.

issues.legal_issue: A claim that acquisition proceedings concerning part of the land lapsed for want of possession and an award fails when the record shows that possession covered the whole land and an award covered the acquisition.
material_facts: A challenger asserted that the authorities had not taken possession of a portion of the acquired land and that no award related to that portion.
The Court found that possession of the entire land had been delivered to the authority and that the proceeding of 31 July 1984 was an award in substance.
issues.conclusion: The contention that proceedings relating to a portion of the land had lapsed was rejected as contrary to the record.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 17(1), 11 and 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, taking possession under the urgency procedure vests the land, and the Court found that the award proceeding covered the acquisition. The Court also relied on the prior decision in Ajodhya Bhagat v. State of Bihar, AIR 1974 SC 1886, in concluding that the contention about possession was against the record.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and party_claims_partial_nonpossession and record_shows_entire_land_delivered and award_covers_acquisition

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns proceedings to acquire land.
predicates.party_claims_partial_nonpossession: A party asserts that possession was not taken of part of the land covered by the acquisition.
predicates.record_shows_entire_land_delivered: The record establishes that possession of the whole acquired land was delivered to the acquiring authority.
predicates.award_covers_acquisition: An award in substance relates to the acquisition at issue.

issues.definition: A claim of lapse based on alleged nonpossession of part of the land is rejected when the record establishes delivery of the whole land and an award covering the acquisition.
